paras: The lynching of Frank Davis was the hanging of a Black man by masked men in the court-house yard at Tupelo, Mississippi, early on June 19, 1888. Davis, charged with an attempted rape of a girl at Saltillo, was taken from the Lee County jail after the lynchers seized Sheriff Long. Memphis and Mississippi papers carried the story under the headline "A Negro Rapist Lynched," and later counted it among three lynchings in the state in one week.

According to a Memphis Avalanche special from Tupelo, Davis, a "negro boy" of about 20, was accused of attacking Lou Fields, an 11-year-old orphan living with Gen. McAllister of Saltillo, on the morning of June 18. The wire version described him as a stranger who had been "loafing around Saltillo" for several days and said he came from Starkville. Both accounts said the girl's screams drew men who were passing, though the wire had them capture Davis on the spot, while the Avalanche said he fled and was caught soon afterward. The wire also asserted, without naming a source, that he "admitted the attempted outrage."

Davis was brought to Tupelo and lodged in the county jail on June 18. About 1 o'clock that night, a man roused Sheriff Long, claiming that he and others had brought in a prisoner from McCarthy's, east of town. When the sheriff reached the jail, he was seized and his keys taken; the Avalanche special put the party at fifteen masked men. The men took Davis from his cell and hanged him from the limb of a tree in the court-house yard.

The wire closed with the line "No clews to the identity of the lynchers," and no report of an inquest, arrest or grand jury action appears in the coverage. Within days, the Greenville Times and the Chickasaw Messenger noted one lynching in Lee County and two in Adams County that week, all of Black men charged with assaults on women.

Only white papers covered the lynching, and they accepted the accusation as fact. The Memphis Appeal ran the Tupelo wire on June 20 under the decks "A Negro Rapist Lynched" and "A Mob Plays a Ruse on a Mississippi Sheriff," saying the prisoner "Had Outraged a Little Girl." The Macon Beacon reprinted the same dispatch on June 23 as "Negro Rapist Lynched."

The Iuka Reporter instead printed the Memphis Avalanche special on June 21, which supplied the names of Davis and the girl and called the alleged attack his "helish purpose." Later Mississippi notices reduced the case to a single line; the Greenville Times wrote that "All were negroes and all for the same kind of crime," and the Chickasaw Messenger described the charge as "criminal assault upon unprotected females." None of these papers criticized the lynchers.

The two Tupelo dispatches differ in detail rather than substance: only the Avalanche gave the number of lynchers and mentioned masks, and only the wire described the ruse on the sheriff and the claimed admission.

reader.title: Lynching of Frank Davis
bases: A party of men took a jailed Black prisoner from the Lee County jail at Tupelo after seizing the sheriff and hanged him in the court-house yard (A1, A2).

Davis was hanged by men who overpowered the sheriff and took him from jail without any legal process, fifteen masked men in one account and 'the party' in the other, in punishment for an accused attempted rape (A1, A2); later state papers counted it among the week's lynchings (A5, A6).

Two separately written Tupelo dispatches, the wire in the Memphis Appeal and the Memphis Avalanche special reprinted at Iuka, agree on the jail seizure and the hanging in the court-house yard (A1, A2), and two Mississippi papers later listed a lynching in Lee County (A5, A6).

accounts.label: Tupelo wire (Memphis Appeal)
accounts.gist: A man roused Sheriff Long with a story of a prisoner brought from McCarthy's; at the jail the sheriff was seized, the keys taken, and Davis hanged in the court-house yard. The wire claims Davis admitted the attempt and that no clues to the lynchers were found.

accounts.label: Memphis Avalanche special
accounts.gist: Names Frank Davis and the girl Lou Fields; says Davis fled, was soon captured, and that fifteen masked men overpowered the sheriff, took the cell key and hanged him from a tree limb in the court-house yard.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal headlined 'A Negro Rapist Lynched' and 'A Mob Plays a Ruse on a Mississippi Sheriff', stating as fact that the prisoner 'Had Outraged a Little Girl'.
The Macon Beacon ran the same wire under 'Negro Rapist Lynched.'
The Iuka Reporter's Avalanche text called the alleged attempt Davis's 'helish purpose' and described the girl's guardian as 'a highly respected citizen'.
The Greenville Times and Chickasaw Messenger noted the Lee County lynching in a single sentence alongside two in Adams County, stressing the crime charged.

record_check.dossier: The hanging took place about 1 a.m. on June 19, 1888; June 18 was the day of the alleged attempt and the jailing.
An unorganized group of masked men, called a 'mob' and a 'party'; no organized band is named.
